title: “INTOXICATED WITH HER LOVE”: THE BIBLE IS MORE POSITIVE ABOUT MARITAL DESIRE THAN MANY CHRISTIANS REALIZE
paragraphs: “INTOXICATED WITH HER LOVE”: THE BIBLE IS MORE POSITIVE ABOUT MARITAL DESIRE THAN MANY CHRISTIANS REALIZE
What if some Christians have spent years feeling ashamed of something God Himself told a husband and wife to enjoy?
There is a sentence in the Bible so intimate that, if you heard it quoted without knowing where it came from, you might wonder whether it belonged in Scripture at all.
But it does.
Not hidden in some obscure manuscript.
Not smuggled into the text by a modern culture obsessed with sex.
It sits in the wisdom literature of the Old Testament, surrounded by warnings against adultery, spoken precisely because God cares about holiness.
The Hebrew says:
“אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד”
“A loving doe, a graceful mountain goat. Let her breasts satisfy you at all times; be infatuated with her love always.” — Proverbs 5:19
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because generations of Christians have sometimes spoken about marital sexuality with embarrassment while Scripture itself can speak about it with remarkable warmth.
The final Hebrew words are especially striking:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
“With her love, be continually captivated.”

The verb שָׁגָה — shagah — can carry the idea of wandering, reeling, being intoxicated or overwhelmed. In Proverbs 5:19, the imagery is deliberately intense: the husband is being told not merely to tolerate his wife's affection, but to remain deeply captivated by her love.
That matters.
Because the surrounding context makes the contrast unmistakable.
The same chapter warns a man about sexual unfaithfulness. Proverbs does not answer forbidden desire by declaring all desire filthy. It redirects desire toward covenant faithfulness.
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.” — Proverbs 5:18
Then comes the language of satisfaction, delight and intoxication.
Then immediately:
“Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman?”
Do you see what Scripture is doing?
It does not say, “Stop desiring.”
It essentially says:
Desire faithfully.
Desire covenantally.
Rejoice in the person to whom you have given yourself.
There is an enormous difference between lust that consumes another person and marital desire that delights in a beloved spouse.
One says, “Your body exists for my appetite.”
The other says, “You are my beloved, and I delight in the gift of belonging faithfully to one another.”
One takes.
The other gives.
One objectifies.
The other knows, cherishes, protects and remains.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that because you grew up believing holiness meant becoming almost embarrassed by the body God created.
Maybe nobody ever explained this to you.
Maybe sex was discussed only when somebody sinned.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Fornication.
Pregnancy outside marriage.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
So somewhere along the way, without anyone deliberately teaching it, you absorbed an assumption:
Sex must be dirty because Christians only talk about it when something goes wrong.
Then you got married.
And suddenly you were expected to flip a switch.
Yesterday, desire was something you were terrified of.
Today, somehow, you were supposed to understand how to receive it as a gift.
Nobody told your nervous system that marriage had happened.
Nobody explained that biblical holiness is not hatred of the body.
And maybe the shame followed you into the bedroom.
That is where this gets painfully personal.
Because there are Christian husbands who love Jesus but have never learned tenderness.
There are Christian wives who love Jesus but quietly wonder whether enjoying their husband's desire makes them less spiritual.
There are spouses who share a bed but have stopped sharing their hearts.
There are couples who can pray together in church yet cannot talk honestly about loneliness, affection, rejection, fear or intimacy.
And there are wounded people carrying experiences of coercion, betrayal, pornography, abuse, infidelity or years of emotional neglect.
So this subject cannot be handled carelessly.
Biblical marital desire is never permission for selfishness.
It is never permission for coercion.
It is never permission to weaponize Scripture against a spouse.

And 1 Corinthians 7 is particularly important here because Paul describes marital responsibility with startling mutuality. The husband has obligations toward his wife, and the wife toward her husband. Paul then deliberately mirrors his language: neither spouse is presented as an autonomous consumer of the other's body. His instruction concerning temporary abstinence explicitly includes mutual agreement.
That means biblical intimacy cannot honestly be reduced to:
“You owe me.”
Christian marriage moves toward:
“I give myself to you.”
Those sentences may sound similar to selfish ears.
They are worlds apart.
Jesus Himself gives us the pattern for Christian love—not domination, but self-giving love.
Christ does not teach His people to ask, “How much can I extract from someone who belongs to me?”
The Gospel teaches us to ask, “How can I love faithfully, sacrificially and truthfully?”
This is why marital intimacy, at its healthiest, is larger than physical release.
It becomes another language through which covenant says:
I still choose you.
I see the years on your face.
I know what childbirth did to your body.
I know what age has changed.
I know the insecurities you hide when the lights go out.
I know where you have been wounded.
I know we have argued.
I know we have disappointed each other.
And I am still here.
Still faithful.
Still learning you.
Still choosing you.
Still thankful that God entrusted your heart to my care.
There is something profoundly beautiful about that.
Scripture's celebration of romantic love becomes even more unmistakable in the Song of Songs.

There, husband and wife—or the lovers moving toward and within covenantal union, depending on how particular passages are interpreted—speak with extraordinary delight about one another's appearance, presence, fragrance, touch and desire.
The woman is not portrayed as an emotionless object.
She speaks.
She desires.
She seeks.
She delights.
She is delighted in.
At one breathtaking moment she says:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.” — Song of Songs 7:10
The Hebrew word for “desire” there is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.
That word is rare in the Hebrew Bible.
And here, in this poetry of love, desire is not treated as something inherently degrading. Within the biblical vision of faithful love, it can be received as something beautiful.
This is important because Christianity is not ultimately a religion teaching us that physical creation is evil.
Genesis begins somewhere very different.
God made humanity embodied.
Male and female.
And before sin corrupted anything, Scripture says God's creation was “very good.”
Sin did not invent the body.
God did.
Sin did not invent marriage.
God did.
Sin did not invent the capacity for marital union.
God did.
What sin does is twist gifts away from their Giver and their purpose.
Desire becomes lust.
Attraction becomes exploitation.
Pleasure becomes addiction.
Intimacy becomes manipulation.
Bodies become commodities.
People become images on screens.
Covenant becomes convenience.
And suddenly something created for faithful union becomes another place where human beings hide, use, betray and destroy one another.
That is the scandal.
But the Gospel never ends at the scandal.
Jesus enters the wreckage.
This is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a slogan.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He meets adulterers.
He meets the sexually broken.
He meets the ashamed.
He meets people whose histories cannot be posted publicly.
He meets people carrying memories they wish could be erased.
And Christ does not save us by pretending sin was harmless.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin was so serious that redemption cost blood.
But grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly shed His own.
Jesus did not die so we could rename bondage freedom.
He died to actually free us.
He does not merely cover scandal with religious language.
He transforms sinners.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He teaches us how to love again.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Maybe pornography followed you for years.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe you gave yourself away searching for love and discovered that being wanted is not the same thing as being cherished.
Maybe your marriage looks healthy in photographs but feels painfully distant after everyone goes home.
Maybe you cannot remember the last time your spouse looked at you with tenderness instead of exhaustion.
Maybe desire disappeared under diapers, bills, grief, arguments, medication, insecurity, work, menopause, illness, resentment or years of unresolved hurt.
This article is not telling you to fake passion.
It is telling you something more hopeful.
Your marriage does not have to be discipled by shame.
Bring the truth into the light.
Talk.
Listen.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where wounds are deep.
If there has been abuse or coercion, safety and accountability matter; biblical teaching about marriage must never be used to trap someone in harm.
And if the problem is simply that two people who once adored each other slowly became roommates...
begin again.
Not necessarily with sex.
Begin with seeing.
Put down the phone.
Ask the question you stopped asking.
Touch without demanding.
Listen without fixing.
Apologize without defending yourself.
Tell your wife she is beautiful without making it a transaction.
Tell your husband what you still admire about him before another year disappears.
Pray together even if the first prayer feels awkward.
Laugh again.
Date again.
Flirt again.
Hold hands again.
Learn one another again.
Because covenant love is not merely remembering who someone was when you married them.
It is discovering who they are becoming and choosing to love that person too.
And when marital desire grows inside that soil—trust, tenderness, safety, faithfulness, laughter, forgiveness and covenant—it need not be treated as Christianity's embarrassing relative.
Scripture does not.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
“Be captivated by her love.”
Those words are in your Bible.
Perhaps the church should stop being more embarrassed about God's design than God appears to be.
But we must also refuse the opposite error.
Our culture often treats sexual desire as sovereign.
If you desire it, pursue it.
If attraction changes, leave.
If fulfillment fades, replace the person.
If boundaries frustrate you, boundaries must be oppressive.
The Bible offers something radically different.
Desire is good.
But desire is not God.
Pleasure is good.
But pleasure is not God.
Marriage is good.
But marriage is not God.
Your spouse is precious.
But your spouse cannot be your Savior.
Every human love eventually reveals its limitations.
Bodies age.
Libido changes.
Illness comes.
Beauty changes.
Death separates.
No husband can carry the infinite weight of his wife's soul.
No wife can carry the infinite weight of her husband's soul.
There is a hunger beneath every human hunger that another human being cannot finally satisfy.
That hunger leads us to Christ.
Marriage can whisper something about covenant.
But Jesus is the Bridegroom who never breaks covenant.
Human love can say, “I choose you.”
At Calvary, Christ showed what covenant love ultimately costs.
Human spouses sometimes fail.
Jesus remains faithful.
Human beings sometimes hide when their shame is exposed.
Jesus walked toward the cross carrying ours.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
You may have a past.
Christ has grace.
You may have scars.
Christ has wounds.
You may have secrets.
Christ already knows.
You may have failed sexually, relationally, emotionally or spiritually.
Repentance does not lead you away from Jesus.
It brings you running toward the One who already knew the worst chapter and still went to the cross.
The Christian message is not:
“Good people never become scandals.”
The Christian message is:
Christ saves sinners.
He forgives the guilty.
He restores the broken.
He teaches selfish hearts how to love.
He takes what sin distorted and begins the long work of redemption.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe that is the sentence your marriage needs tonight.
Not another performance.
Not another accusation.
Not another comparison with somebody else's marriage online.
Grace.
Truth.
Repentance.
Tenderness.
Jesus.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded Christian reads at 2:00 in the morning and realizes, “I am not the only one fighting for healing.”
Not because every marriage problem can be solved by rereading a Facebook post, but because shame has a way of making us forget what is true.
Send it privately to the couple who may be struggling behind smiling photographs.
We glorify God through Christ-centered obedience in every area of life.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somewhere in your circle is a husband ashamed to admit his marriage feels cold.
A wife wondering whether God cares about the loneliness beside her in bed.
A believer fighting pornography in secret.
A wounded spouse trying to believe intimacy can ever feel safe again.
A young Christian being taught by culture that biblical holiness means repression.
A married couple who desperately need to remember that covenant is worth fighting for.
And maybe they will never search for an article like this.
Maybe it has to find them through you.
Because Christianity does not teach us to worship desire.
And it does not require married believers to be ashamed of desire either.
It teaches us something far more beautiful.
Let desire bow before Christ.
Let passion live inside covenant.
Let pleasure remain a gift rather than becoming a god.
Let husbands cherish rather than consume.
Let wives be cherished rather than objectified.
Let both spouses give rather than demand.
Let repentance enter the places shame locked shut.
Let grace enter the bedroom.
Let Jesus enter the marriage.
And when He does, do not be surprised if He begins rewriting things you thought were already over.
The marriage you thought was merely surviving.
The affection you assumed had died.
The body you learned to hate.
The past you believed disqualified you.
The shame you carried into marriage.
The secret you finally confessed.
The wound that still needs time.
The love that needs rebuilding.
The sinner who needs forgiving.
The heart that needs returning home.
Maybe the most shocking thing about Proverbs 5:19 is not that the Bible tells a husband to be intoxicated with his wife's love.
Maybe the shocking thing is that the God who knows how badly humanity has distorted love still believes love is worth redeeming.
And perhaps that is what grace has been whispering through this entire story:
What sin distorted, Jesus is not afraid to enter—and what shame told you to bury, Christ may yet redeem.
